claims.text: An integrated rapid-solidification, high-speed calorimetry, in situ X-ray diffraction, and CALPHAD approach can accurately and efficiently determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a wide HEA compositional space.
Conventionally melted HEAs may have coarse microstructures and compositional segregation.
HEAs can be fabricated using SLM or LPBF under argon.
Rapid solidification by SLM or LPBF produces fine-grained, compositionally more homogeneous HEAs.
High-speed DSC can determine HEA melting temperature and fusion enthalpy and entropy.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction during laser melting can characterize HEA melting transitions.
Controlled high heating and cooling rates minimize segregation during HEA melting.
The proposed measurement conditions ensure uniform energy input.
Rapid solidification refines grain size and reduces elemental segregation.
Grain refinement and reduced segregation lower uncertainty in measurements of transition phenomena.
In situ measurements capture phase transitions with high temporal resolution.
Correlating calorimetric signals and diffraction data with CALPHAD simulations allows accurate deduction of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change.
The method will yield melting temperatures within 5–10% of CALPHAD predictions.
Fusion enthalpy and entropy measurements will be reproducible across different HEA compositions.
Traditional DSC on as-cast or conventionally melted HEAs is limited by coarse microstructures and compositional inhomogeneity.
Extreme compositional complexity may limit the applicability of the integrated method.
Ultra-high heating rates may induce nonequilibrium phases that alter melting transitions.
Calibration and detection limits at high heating rates may prevent quantitative agreement with CALPHAD across the entire HEA family.
The volume change at melting can be determined from high-resolution in situ diffraction data.

The approach is to be rejected if all four measured properties consistently differ by more than 10% from an independently verified benchmark across multiple HEAs, or if measurements are not reproducible across rapid-solidification samples.
